explanation: This is the other half of the Williams argument, and the one his critics attacked hardest. The rise of industrial capitalism in Britain is what destroyed the slave trade, the West Indian interest having become an obstacle to a manufacturing economy rather than its engine. The Act of 1807 is where that claim is tested, and the cited account of Capitalism and Slavery says Williams wrote it against a body of history that used the abolition acts as a moral turning point. The atlas records the claim as disputed because the dissent is argued at least as well as the thesis.

dispute.text: Seymour Drescher’s Econocide (1977) is the major attack. He argued that British abolition in 1807 followed from the moral outrage of a British public that could vote, and not from any falling value of slavery to the nation. On his account the trade was killed at its economic peak rather than in its decline. Geggus in 1981 questioned Drescher’s method of valuing capital, and Carrington replied in 1984 that Drescher had misplaced the peak rather than refuted Ragatz and Williams. Nothing in the cited account suggests a settlement.

sources.locator: "Capitalism and Slavery", the criticism of the Williams theses, revision 1341902916
